passages.question: What does the text say about the Tao that can be trodden, and about the name that can be named?
passages.answer: The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What do we call these two aspects together, and where is the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful?
passages.answer: Under these two aspects, it is really the same; but as development takes place, it receives the different names. Together we call them the Mystery. Where the Mystery is the deepest is the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: How do existence and non-existence give birth to one another, and what do difficulty and ease, length and shortness, and height and lowness produce in one another?
passages.answer: So it is that existence and non-existence give birth the one to (the idea of) the other; that difficulty and ease produce the one (the idea of) the other; that length and shortness fashion out the one the figure of the other; that (the ideas of) height and lowness arise from the contrast of the one with the other; that the musical notes and tones become harmonious through the relation of one with another; and that being before and behind give the idea of one following another.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: How does the sage manage affairs, and how does he convey his instructions?
passages.answer: Therefore the sage manages affairs without doing anything, and conveys his instructions without the use of speech.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What does the sage constantly try to keep the people without, and what is universal where there is abstinence from action?
passages.answer: He constantly (tries to) keep them without knowledge and without desire, and where there are those who have knowledge, to keep them from presuming to act (on it). When there is this abstinence from action, good order is universal.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What is the highest excellence like, and what place does it occupy without striving?
passages.answer: The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike. Hence (its way) is near to (that of) the Tao.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: On what does the use of the wheel depend, on what the use of a vessel, and on what the use of an apartment?
passages.answer: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends. Clay is fashioned into vessels; but it is on their empty hollowness, that their use depends. The door and windows are cut out (from the walls) to form an apartment; but it is on the empty space (within), that its use depends. Therefore, what has a (positive) existence serves for profitable adaptation, and what has not that for (actual) usefulness.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What should be brought to the utmost degree, and what is returning to the root called?
passages.answer: The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree, and that of stillness guarded with unwearying vigour. All things alike go through their processes of activity, and (then) we see them return (to their original state). When things (in the vegetable world) have displayed their luxuriant growth, we see each of them return to its root. This returning to their root is what we call the state of stillness; and that stillness may be called a reporting that they have fulfilled their appointed end.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What would follow if we could renounce our sageness and discard our wisdom, renounce our benevolence and discard our righteousness, and renounce our artful contrivances and discard our scheming for gain?
passages.answer: If we could renounce our sageness and discard our wisdom, it would be better for the people a hundredfold. If we could renounce our benevolence and discard our righteousness, the people would again become filial and kindly. If we could renounce our artful contrivances and discard our (scheming for) gain, there would be no thieves nor robbers.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What becomes of the partial, the crooked, the empty, and the worn out, and who gets his desires and who goes astray?
passages.answer: The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new. He whose (desires) are few gets them; he whose (desires) are many goes astray.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What does the sage hold in his embrace, and why can no one in the world strive with him?
passages.answer: Therefore the sage holds in his embrace the one thing (of humility), and manifests it to all the world. He is free from self-display, and therefore he shines; from self-assertion, and therefore he is distinguished; from self-boasting, and therefore his merit is acknowledged; from self-complacency, and therefore he acquires superiority. It is because he is thus free from striving that therefore no one in the world is able to strive with him.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What was there, undefined and complete, coming into existence before Heaven and Earth?
passages.answer: There was something undefined and complete, coming into existence before Heaven and Earth. How still it was and formless, standing alone, and undergoing no change, reaching everywhere and in no danger (of being exhausted)! It may be regarded as the Mother of all things.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What does the text say about arms, however beautiful, and who do not like to employ them?
passages.answer: Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen, hateful, it may be said, to all creatures. Therefore they who have the Tao do not like to employ them.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: Who is discerning, and who is intelligent? Who is strong, and who is mighty?
passages.answer: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent. He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty. He who is satisfied with his lot is rich; he who goes on acting with energy has a (firm) will.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: In its regular course, what does the Tao do, and what is there that it does not do?
passages.answer: The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of doing it), and so there is nothing which it does not do.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: How does the movement of the Tao proceed, and what marks the course of its mighty deeds? From what did all things under heaven spring?
passages.answer: The movement of the Tao By contraries proceeds; And weakness marks the course Of Tao's mighty deeds. All things under heaven sprang from It as existing (and named); that existence sprang from It as non-existent (and not named).
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What is the softest thing in the world, and what does it dash against and overcome?
passages.answer: The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the hardest; that which has no (substantial) existence enters where there is no crevice. I know hereby what advantage belongs to doing nothing (with a purpose).
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: Or fame or life, Which do you hold more dear? Or life or wealth, To which would you adhere? Keep life and lose those other things; Keep them and lose your life:--which brings Sorrow and pain more near?
passages.answer: Thus we may see, Who cleaves to fame Rejects what is more great; Who loves large stores Gives up the richer state. Who is content Needs fear no shame. Who knows to stop Incurs no blame. From danger free Long live shall he.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: There is no guilt greater than what, no calamity greater than what, and no fault greater than what?
passages.answer: There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition; no calamity greater than to be discontented with one's lot; no fault greater than the wish to be getting. Therefore the sufficiency of contentment is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What does one understand without going outside his door, and what does one see without looking out from his window?
passages.answer: Without going outside his door, one understands (all that takes place) under the sky; without looking out from his window, one sees the Tao of Heaven. The farther that one goes out (from himself), the less he knows.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: He who devotes himself to learning seeks from day to day to increase what, and he who devotes himself to the Tao seeks to diminish what?
passages.answer: He who devotes himself to learning (seeks) from day to day to increase (his knowledge); he who devotes himself to the Tao (seeks) from day to day to diminish (his doing).
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: Who does not care to speak about the Tao, and who does not know it?
passages.answer: He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he who is (ever ready to) speak about it does not know it.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What has a sage said he will do, and what will the people do of themselves?
passages.answer: Therefore a sage has said, 'I will do nothing (of purpose), and the people will be transformed of themselves; I will be fond of keeping still, and the people will of themselves become correct. I will take no trouble about it, and the people will of themselves become rich; I will manifest no ambition, and the people will of themselves attain to the primitive simplicity.'
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: Governing a great state is like what?
passages.answer: Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: Why are the rivers and seas able to receive the homage and tribute of all the valley streams, and what does the sage do who wishes to be above men?
passages.answer: That whereby the rivers and seas are able to receive the homage and tribute of all the valley streams, is their skill in being lower than they;--it is thus that they are the kings of them all. So it is that the sage (ruler), wishing to be above men, puts himself by his words below them, and, wishing to be before them, places his person behind them.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What are the three precious things which the author prizes and holds fast?
passages.answer: But I have three precious things which I prize and hold fast. The first is gentleness; the second is economy; and the third is shrinking from taking precedence of others.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What is the highest attainment, and what is a disease?
passages.answer: To know and yet (think) we do not know is the highest (attainment); not to know (and yet think) we do know is a disease.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: To what is the Way of Heaven compared, and what does it do where there is superabundance and where there is deficiency?
passages.answer: May not the Way (or Tao) of Heaven be compared to the (method of) bending a bow? The (part of the bow) which was high is brought low, and what was low is raised up. (So Heaven) diminishes where there is superabundance, and supplements where there is deficiency.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What is there in the world more soft and weak than water, and what can take precedence of it for attacking things that are firm and strong?
passages.answer: There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water, and yet for attacking things that are firm and strong there is nothing that can take precedence of it;--for there is nothing (so effectual) for which it can be changed.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)

passages.question: What does the text say about sincere words and fine words, and about those who are skilled in the Tao and those who dispute about it?
passages.answer: Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere. Those who are skilled (in the Tao) do not dispute (about it); the disputatious are not skilled in it. Those who know (the Tao) are not extensively learned; the extensively learned do not know it.
passages.source: Tao Te Ching, translated by James Legge (Project Gutenberg 216)
